Your workplace: when you get a regular job (waiter, factory worker, salesperson, bricklayer, farmhand, office worker, civil servant, police officer, technician, teacher, programmer, engineer, lawyer or doctor), the company or institution is generated: name, size, formal or informal, whether there’s a union, your boss and 4 to 8 coworkers with a trait and a relationship; one of them is your rival.
Performance: each month it moves toward a target that depends on your skill in the trade, your hours, your relationship with your boss, your certification, your seniority, your stress and your health. Every 6 months there’s a review with a bonus, a raise, a warning or dismissal.
Promotions: each trade has its own ladder. You only move up when a real opening appears; you apply with a visible probability. Some positions require a certification (the specialty for a specialist doctor, for example).
Real conditions by country: legal working week, overtime pay, vacation, year-end bonus, severance, unions and informality. Check the Conditions tab.
And also: offers from competitors you can use to negotiate, asking for a raise, night shifts, accidents in risky trades, stress and burnout, and conversations with consequences (covering a shift, layoff rumors, a boss who humiliates you, gossip, urgent projects).
It’s the maximum number of hours a week the law allows as a normal working week. Most countries use 40 hours; Mexico, 48 (a reform is on the way to cut it to 40); France, 35.
In the game, your country’s hours set how much each overtime hour is worth.
Work beyond the legal week is paid at a premium: in Mexico, double; in the US, 1.5 times. Some countries set no premium and leave it to contracts.
With «Overtime» you work about 8 more hours a week: your performance, stress and salary go up.
Days off with pay. They vary a lot: the US doesn’t require them; Brazil gives 30 days; Mexico gives 12 the first year, rising with seniority.
Each week of vacation gives you free time and lowers your stress a lot. Informal jobs don’t pay it.
A mandatory additional yearly payment in many countries: in Mexico, at least 15 days of pay in December; in Brazil and Argentina, a full month; in Spain, two extra payments.
You get it at year end if your job is formal, in proportion to the months worked.
Compensation the company pays when it fires you without just cause. In Mexico it’s 3 months of pay plus 20 days per year worked; in the US it isn’t mandatory.
If you’re fired from a formal job, you get it according to your country’s law and your seniority.
A union negotiates on behalf of workers: wages, hours and conditions (collective agreement). In the Nordic countries more than half of workers are members; in Mexico, about 12 %.
If there’s a union at your job, a collective agreement is signed every year that raises everyone’s pay. Joining costs 1 % of your salary and gives you someone to turn to in a conflict.
Work without a contract or social security. In Mexico it’s more than half of all jobs; in rich countries, less than 15 %. It’s most common in farming, construction and small services.
An informal job gives no year-end bonus, paid vacation or severance, and almost never has a union.
A formal job is registered: you pay into social security (health, pension, housing) and have the rights of labor law.
It’s decided when you’re hired, based on your country and your trade.
Companies evaluate their staff on targets, hours, quality and how they treat others. A good review brings raises; several bad ones, dismissal.
Every 6 months there’s a review: 80 or more is excellent (bonus and raise), 65 good, 50 fair, below 50 poor (warning). With 2 warnings and another poor review, you’re fired.
Chronic stress lowers productivity and health. Extreme exhaustion (burnout) is recognized by the WHO as an occupational phenomenon.
It rises with overtime, night shifts and risky trades; it falls with vacations and getting along with others. Above 85 you start losing health.
The time you’ve been with the company. In many countries it increases your vacation, your severance and your chances of promotion.
It adds to your performance and to your chance of winning an opening.
Night and rotating shifts disrupt sleep and increase fatigue; in some countries they’re paid better.
Night and rotating shifts raise your stress every month.
The ladder of positions in a trade. To move up you need a real opening: someone retires, quits, gets fired or the company grows.
When an opening appears you can apply. Your chance depends on your performance, seniority, certification, relationship with your boss and your rival’s level.
